drills.q: 100M DAU, 20 requests per user per day. Average and peak QPS, and what would you size with each?
drills.a: 1e8 x 2e1 = 2e9/day / 1e5 s = 2e4 = 20,000 QPS average; peak at 2-3x for a global consumer product is 40-60k QPS. Peak sustained sizes the fleet and database; peak burst sizes the queue, connection pool, and rate limiter; peak concurrent (throughput x latency) sizes memory and file descriptors. Sanity: 20k QPS of JSON is 20-40 stateless nodes, unremarkable.

drills.q: Recite the latency ladder from L1 to cross-Pacific, then state the three ratios.
drills.a: L1 1 ns, L2 4 ns, L3 ~12 ns, DDR5 RAM 50-80 ns, 1 KB compress 1-3 us, NVMe random read 20-100 us, SATA SSD 100-200 us, same-DC RTT ~0.5 ms, cross-AZ 1-2 ms, HDD seek 5-10 ms, US east-west 60-70 ms, US-Europe 75-90 ms, US-APAC 170-230 ms, LLM first token 300-800 ms. Ratios: RAM ~1000x SSD; same-DC RTT ~1000x RAM; cross-continent ~100-300x same-DC.

drills.q: Convert 99.99% into a design constraint, then compute the SLO of five serial services each at 99.99%.
drills.a: 99.99% is 53 minutes/year, 4.3 minutes/month, which means no human in the recovery path: automatic health-checked failover, and the deploy pipeline becomes a primary risk since a bad deploy plus manual rollback exceeds the monthly budget. Five serial services at 99.99% give 0.9999^5 = ~99.95%, about 4.4 hours/year, and independence is false anyway (shared network, control plane, deploy pipeline), so the real number is worse. Fix by removing hops from the critical path, not by making five hops more reliable.

drills.q: Storage for 1M records/day at 1 KB with 5-year retention. Give the full chain and then tier it.
drills.a: 1e6 x 1e3 B = 1 GB/day; x 365 x 5 = 1.8 TB logical; x3 replication = 5.5 TB; +30% index = ~7 TB; plus WAL and backups, so 10-14 TB provisioned. Formula: records x bytes x retention x replication x (1 + index). Tier it because ~90% of reads hit recent data: hot months on NVMe, older partitions on cheap storage, beyond the query horizon in S3/Parquet via an external table. Name the boundary as a number.

drills.q: 50M DAU social feed: reads, writes, peak, payload bandwidth, and the number that actually breaks.
drills.a: Reads 5e7 x 10 = 5e8/day / 1e5 = 5,000 QPS avg; writes 5e7 x 1 = 500 QPS avg; peak x3 gives 15,000 and 1,500. Payload 20 items x 300 B = 6 KB, so 15,000 x 6 KB = 90 MB/s = 720 Mbps egress. The number that breaks: amplified writes = 500 posts/s x 500 followers = 250,000 timeline inserts/s. 1,500 write QPS is one Postgres primary; 250k inserts/s is why fanout is async.

drills.q: 15,000 peak QPS, 20 ms service time, 5 ms CPU per request. How many servers, computed two ways?
drills.a: Little's Law: concurrency = 1.5e4 x 2e-2 = 300 in flight, trivial for async, ~2-3 instances for thread-per-request. CPU: 1 core at 100% = 200 rps, at a 60% target 120 rps/core, so 1.5e4/1.2e2 = 125 cores = 16 x 8-core; x1.5 to survive losing one of three AZs = ~24 instances. The methods disagree 10x and CPU wins, because Little's Law bounds concurrency, not throughput. If service time becomes 2 s (an LLM call), concurrency is 30,000 in flight, thread-per-request is impossible, and file descriptors and provider rate limits bind instead of CPU.

drills.q: How much Redis for 50M users' timelines at 800 entries of 40 bytes? Then reduce it.
drills.a: Naive payload: 5e7 x 8e2 x 4e1 = 1.6e12 B = 1.6 TB, and that is ~3x low. Redis adds 50-100 B per key and a zset past 128 members becomes a skiplist at ~80-120 B/member, so realistically ~4.4 TB. Reduce: cache only 7-day-active users (~40%) to ~1.8 TB; cut the cap 800 to 200 entries (ten pages covers >95% of sessions) to ~450 GB; pack the member into 8 bytes to ~250 GB. That is 6-12 shards, ~$3-6k/month, not $60k. Verify with MEMORY USAGE and OBJECT ENCODING.

drills.q: Egress bill for a photo service: 500M DAU, 50 views/day, 200 KB each. Then drop the CDN hit rate from 95% to 90%.
drills.a: 5e8 x 5e1 = 2.5e10 views/day x 2e5 B = 5 PB/day, ~150 PB/month; bandwidth 50 GB/s = 400 Gbps avg, ~1.2 Tbps peak. At list $0.05/GB that is $7.5M/month; negotiated at $0.005-0.01/GB it is $0.75-1.5M, a 5-10x contract lever. Compute is negligible (~375 cores for transform-on-miss), so egress is 10-100x the compute bill. Dropping the hit rate 95% to 90% DOUBLES origin load, because origin traffic scales with (1 - hit_rate). The usual cause is cache fragmentation from arbitrary on-demand image widths, which is the real reason to restrict transforms to fixed sizes.

drills.q: Size storage for a messaging system at 100B messages/day, and name the one requirement that changes the answer by four orders of magnitude.
drills.a: 1e11/day / 1e5 = 1M messages/s avg, 3M/s peak; amplified deliveries at ~3 recipients = 3M/s avg, ~10M/s peak. If server-side history is required: ~300 B/message x 1e11 = 30 TB/day, x3 replication = 90 TB/day, ~33 PB/year. If the client is the source of truth and messages are deleted on delivery, only the undelivered backlog persists: ~1% over a one-day offline window = 1e9 x 300 B = 300 GB, which fits in memory. That is ~30,000x, driven by one product question. WhatsApp took the second branch; Slack and Teams take the first because they want server-side search. Also: 2B users at 20% concurrency is 4e8 persistent connections, ~8,000 nodes at 50k conns each, which is the actually hard part rather than the byte volume.

drills.q: Cost a RAG support assistant at 1M conversations/day, 6 turns, 4k input + 300 output tokens, then make it viable and order the levers by risk.
drills.a: Input 2.4e10 = 24,000 M tokens/day x $2/M = $48k/day; output 1.8e9 = 1,800 M x $10/M = $18k/day; ~$66k/day = ~$2M/month, unviable. Embeddings are 3e8 tokens/day at ~$0.02/M = $6/day, so retrieval is free relative to generation and must not be optimised first. Levers: prompt caching (~80% of input is a stable prefix, cache reads ~10% of input price) ~3.6x; context diet from 4k to 1.5k via top-3 reranking ~2.7x; model routing of the easy 70% to a Flash-class model at ~20x cheaper ~2.5x; Batch API -50% for non-interactive. Composed ~24x to ~$80k/month. Ship caching and context reduction first (no quality coupling) and routing last, since a wrong route on a billing question is a support escalation.

drills.q: Size a vector index for 100M chunks at 1024 dimensions, and say which is more expensive, building or serving.
drills.a: float32: 1e8 x 1024 x 4 B = 410 GB; HNSW M=32 stores up to 64 layer-0 neighbour ids at 4 B plus upper layers, ~300 B/node = 30 GB; ~440 GB total and it must be RAM-resident, so ~600 GB with headroom = 3-4 shards of 256 GB. int8 quantisation gives 4x (~132 GB, one node) at 1-2 recall points, recoverable by over-fetching top-50 and reranking against float32. Binary gives 32x (~13 GB) with an NVMe float32 rerank of the top-100. Cost ~$5,000/month to ~$700/month, a 7x lever. Serving beats building by ~40x: embedding 100M chunks at ~400 tokens = 4e10 tokens at ~$0.02/M is ~$800 one-time versus $700-5,000/month forever. So the sizing question is a MEMORY question, and re-embedding the corpus with a better model is cheap.

drills.q: Name a number you would refuse to estimate, and say how you make a decision without it.
drills.a: p99.9 latency, or anything driven by variance rather than volume: queueing under bursty arrival, GC pauses, lock contention, noisy neighbours, retry amplification. Also anything within 2-3x of a hard cliff (a memory boundary, a provider rate limit, an SLO edge), because there a 3x error changes the architecture. Instead of predicting the tail, design so the tail cannot hurt you: a timeout well inside the budget, a bulkhead so one slow dependency cannot consume the fleet, a queue so bursts become latency instead of errors, and an explicit load-shedding rule.
